title: Video | Copper versus aluminium: is the substitution story overblown? | Wood Mackenzie
gist: Wood Mackenzie's Alex Griffiths and Charles Cooper argue that despite surging copper prices reviving the copper-to-aluminium substitution narrative, real substitution is slower and more limited than headline price ratios suggest, because engineering, reliability and performance constraints keep copper hard to displace in EVs, data centres and power infrastructure.

insights.claim: Rising copper prices have reignited a market narrative that manufacturers will substitute aluminium for copper across electric vehicles, power networks, data centres and consumer products, but Wood Mackenzie argues this substitution story is likely overblown relative to headline expectations.
insights.speaker: Alex Griffiths
insights.so_what: Investors pricing in rapid demand destruction for copper from substitution should temper those expectations, supporting a more resilient long-term copper demand case.
insights.quote: Why rising copper prices haven't triggered the widespread demand destruction many expect

insights.claim: The copper-to-aluminium price ratio alone does not capture the real drivers or pace of substitution, because product performance, reliability and engineering requirements make switching materials more complex than price signals imply.
insights.speaker: Alex Griffiths
insights.so_what: Analysts and investors should avoid using simple copper/aluminium price ratios as a proxy for imminent demand shifts; the real substitution signal lags price moves substantially.
insights.quote: While higher copper prices can encourage manufacturers to reduce copper intensity over time, the realities of product performance, reliability and engineering requirements often make substitution more complex than headlines suggest.

insights.claim: Substitution away from copper, where it happens, typically takes years rather than months to feed through into end markets, meaning near-term copper demand is more resilient to price spikes than headline narratives suggest.
insights.speaker: Alex Griffiths
insights.so_what: Investors should not expect a fast demand response to copper price spikes; short-term copper demand elasticity to price is low, supporting near-term price strength.
insights.quote: Why substitution often takes years rather than months to materialise

insights.claim: Manufacturers are responding to higher copper prices primarily by reducing copper intensity in designs rather than eliminating copper altogether, a gradual efficiency response rather than wholesale material switching.
insights.speaker: Alex Griffiths
insights.so_what: This points to a demand growth deceleration rather than demand destruction for copper, a more bullish long-term setup for copper producers than a full substitution thesis implies.
insights.quote: How manufacturers reduce copper intensity without eliminating copper altogether

insights.claim: Copper remains structurally difficult to replace in applications underpinning electrification, digital infrastructure (including data centres) and industrial growth, keeping copper demand resilient even as prices rise.
insights.speaker: Alex Griffiths
insights.so_what: Structural copper demand from electrification and data centre buildout should be viewed as sticky, reinforcing a bullish long-term copper demand thesis relevant to copper miners and related equities.
insights.quote: The discussion explores why copper remains difficult to replace across many applications that underpin electrification, digital infrastructure and industrial growth.
